title: Linking multipoint folding and stability with functional regulation in the mitochondrial transmembrane β-barrel Sam50

paper_content.abstract:
Mitochondrial outer membrane proteins (β-OMPs) serve as the first line of communication with the
cellular milieu. A crucial β-OMP, the sorting and assembly machinery Sam50, is a 16-stranded
transmembrane β-barrel highly conserved in all eukaryotes. Sam50 dysregulation is lethal; yet,
molecular elements that regulate Sam50 remain poorly understood. Here, we identify and characterize
residues that regulate Sam50 structure and function. Using single-molecule electrophysiology, in vivo
function, and stability measurements, we demonstrate that the POlypeptide-TRansport Associated
domain is dispensable for Sam50. Complete characterization of the folding mechanism using 165
Xaa→Ala substitutions reveals that Sam50 folds through parallel pathways, with at least two transition
states. The folding nucleus is towards the N-terminus, whereas frustrated folding at the C-terminal
region kinetically traps the structure. We correlate this unexpected folding of Sam50 with its SAM-
assisted assembly. Additionally, our per-residue stability measurements show that destabilizing hotspots
in Sam50 are linked to its gating function. Our findings suggest how the dynamic structure of Sam50
offers a functional advantage, with specific residues that regulate folding, stability, and function, also
determine the protein’s sensitivity to mutations.
paper_content.introduction:
Mitochondria, the site of cellular bioenergetics, are dual-membrane organelles. The
mitochondrial outer membrane (mOM) is uniquely enriched with transmembrane β-barrel OM proteins
(β-OMPs). β-OMPs regulate metabolite flux, transport ions, proteins, and lipids, form mitochondrial-
endoplasmic reticulum (ER) contacts, and maintain mitostasis.1 β-OMPs are nuclear-encoded and
cytosolically synthesized. They are then imported into the intermembrane space (IMS) of mitochondria,
where they undergo a highly regulated directional insertion into the mOM. This β-OMP insertion is
mediated by the Sorting and Assembly Machinery (SAM).2-4 Sam50, the core SAM component, is a 16-
stranded β-OMP that facilitates substrate insertion into the mOM, with one N-terminal POlypeptide
TRansport Associated (POTRA) domain located in the IMS that mediates precursor release (Figure
1a).2,5,6 Yeast Sam50 additionally binds to peripheral subunits Sam35/Sam37 through its cytosolic
loops.3,4 Sam50 differs functionally from ATP-dependent chaperones in its ability to scaffold the folding
of nascent β-OMPs (including itself) independent of electrochemical energy and membrane
composition. In humans, Sam50 also regulates mitochondrial dynamics, and is involved in lipid
scrambling and mitochondrial quality control.1,7,8 These features render Sam50 essential for
mitochondrial biogenesis and mitochondrial integrity, with defects in Sam50 function linked to
mitochondrial disorders.9

Insights into how the complex process of yeast Sam50-mediated β-OMP folding has been
obtained from a stable structural intermediate captured using cryo-EM.3,4 Here, the β1 seam of the
Sam50 transmembrane domain (TMD) associates dynamically with β16 (Figure 1a). This association
allows β1 to template the C→N assembly of nascent β-OMPs into the mOM. The N-terminal lateral
gate (β1-β3) undergoes structural interconversion between gate-closed (resting) and gate-open
(substrate-bound) states, while the POTRA domain and Sam35/37 remain unaltered.3,4,10,11 Interestingly,
however, the thermodynamics regulating such structural dynamics remains poorly understood. More
importantly, the mechanism of how Sam50 itself folds, the folding pathways adopted by Sam50, and the
residue-specific regulation of transition state structures, remain unclear.

Here, we present details linking Sam50 folding, stability, and function. We show that Sam50
TMD folds and functions independent of its POTRA domain, SAM complex, and Sam35/37. The
folding is stepwise, directed by the primary sequence, and proceeds through parallel pathways. The
transition state structures are similar, where strands β3-β6 nucleates folding, followed by β7-β11
assembly. Residues at β13-β15, form non-native interactions, exhibit late assembly, but are vital for
Sam50 function in vivo. Our findings suggest spontaneous membrane insertion of the pre-assembled N-
terminal strands, and a SAM complex-assisted insertion of the C-terminal strands. Folded Sam50 is
destabilized thermodynamically at β4-β6, and this is mechanistically relevant for the “open↔closed”
interconversion of the Sam50 lateral gate during its function. We suggest this stability-function trade-off
as a possible advantage allowing Sam50 to efficiently fold nascent β-barrels, while also performing
additional essential functions in the mitochondrial membrane.
paper_content.results:
Folding and function of POTRA-less Sam50 resembles full-length Sam50
Sam50 is believed to have evolved from the primordial β-barrel assembly machinery (BamA-
BAM) of Gram-negative bacteria. Here, all extramembranous POTRA domains (except one) are non-
essential for mitochondrial Sam50 function.5 First, we asked if the TMD was sufficient for Sam50
folding, stability, and function. To address this, we generated a POTRA-less variant of yeast Sam50
(Sam50Δ120, only TMD; referred to hereafter as Sam50) (Figure 1a). We examined if the structural and
functional features of the full-length Sam50 (Sam50FL) were retained in POTRA-less Sam50. Similar to
observations with Neurospora crassa Tob55,6 BamA12 and other β-OMPs,13,14 both Sam50FL and
Sam50Δ120 can fold spontaneously in artificial membranes without SAM assistance (Figures S1-S5).
Screens of folding and stability of both proteins in large unilamellar vesicles (LUVs) yielded PC:PE
LUVs (90% DMPC, 10% DMPE) as optimal for path-independent assembly (details in SI Methods,
Table S1).

Folded Sam50 in PC:PE membranes resists proteolysis by proteinase K, and forms a β-rich
structure as revealed by far-UV circular dichroism spectropolarimetry (comparable to NcTob556 and 16-
stranded EcOmpF15). Folded Sam50 also shows a 10 nm blue shift in Trp fluorescence to 336 nm, with
a twofold increase in fluorescence intensity (Figures 1b-e, S1-S6). These observations show that Sam50
can fold into a stable β-barrel independent of its POTRA domain. Sam50 has no identified role in
conducting ions; yet, it can exhibit channel-like behavior in electrophysiology experiments (Figures 1f-
h; S1e-p), with unknown in vivo significance.6,11,16 Comparison of both full-length and POTRA-less
constructs using single molecule electrophysiology6,11, 13,16 revealed channel-like transitions between two
conductance states O1 and O2 (Figure 1f), as reported earlier,11 with the removal of POTRA favoring
the lower conductance O1 state in Sam50Δ120. Both proteins also exhibit similar changes in voltage-
dependent conductance (Figure 1g), and step-wise channel insertion events (Figure 1h). We additionally
validated the in vivo function of Sam50 by complementation of yeast lacking the nuclear-encoded
SAM50. Survival of cells carrying pFL39-SAM50FL and pFL39-SAM50Δ120 was similar in both
fermentable (glucose) and non-fermentable (glycerol) carbon sources at permissive (25 °C, 30 °C) and
non-permissive (37 °C) temperatures (Figure 1i). Taken together, our results show that the TMD is
sufficient for Sam50 folding and function, both in vitro and in vivo.

Sam50 exhibits thermodynamic stability in PC:PE membranes
In β-barrel membrane proteins, several factors determine thermodynamic stability, reversible
folding, and stepwise assembly: (i) the intrinsic ϕ-ψ preferences (β-sheet propensity), (ii) backbone H-
bonding strength of transmembrane residues, and (iii) side chain hydration of lumen-facing residues and
hydropathy of lipid-facing residues.17 The complex interplay between Sam50 and LUVs precludes a
simple interpretation of its thermodynamic parameters. Hence, to deduce the apparent change18,19 in
Gibbs free energy (∆𝐺0) upon Sam50 folding, we monitored Trp fluorescence across 0.67-5.39 M
GdnHCl as the chemical perturbant. We obtained slow microscopic
reversibility and two-state Sam50 (un)folding in lipid:protein ratios of ~1600:1 (~6 proteins per LUV) at
28 °C in PC:PE LUVs (Figure 2a, S7).

Unlike bacterial OMPs,18-22 we found that Sam50 β-barrel is less stable thermodynamically. We
measured a ∆𝐺0,WT of –6.66±0.04 kcal mol-1, a folding cooperativity (M ) of –3.01 kcal mol-1 M-1, and a
mid-point of chemical denaturation (C ) of 2.21±0.01 M (Table S2). Next, we generated a library of
165 Xaa→Ala substitutions in the TMD (Figure 2b), and deduced the contribution of each side chain to
β-barrel stability, by measuring the energetics for each variant (∆𝐺0,Mut) (Figures 2c, S7-S8, Table S2).
The lower entropic cost of introducing Ala (with fewer rotamers) provided us with a per-residue
thermodynamic map of Sam50 (Figures 2d, S9). Here, most substitutions did not alter the overall β-
barrel stability. Despite its moderate stability, we found that the Sam50 structure is tolerant to point
mutations.

Intrinsically destabilizing Sam50 residues (∆∆𝐺0 > +0.45 kcal mol-1) primarily involve Gly, Pro,
and polar residues (Figure 2d, maroon). They are distributed in the β-barrel’s lipid and lumen face,
midplane, and the interface, and are marginally higher at β4-β6. Specifically, Ser, Thr, Asn, and Gln
destabilize Sam50 when they are located at β1-β8 lumen over β9-β16. We inferred that such a polarized
destabilization localized at the N-terminal strands correlates with Sam50 function. Opening of Sam50
lateral gate,4 and repositioning of β1-β3 in the mOM for substrate assembly, requires hinge-like
conformational displacement at β4-β6. Therefore, strategically positioned residues at β4-β6 with
lowered stability (Figure 2d, highlighted region), could facilitate the interconversion of “closed” and
“open” states of Sam50. Supporting our observation, we found only two residues (W240, F455) as
intrinsically stabilizing (∆∆𝐺0 < –0.45 kcal mol-1). Other transmembrane aromatic residues do not alter
Sam50 stability (Table S2), suggesting that the contribution of W240 and F455 is location-specific.
Our experiments show S170 (β4), N175 (β4), N415 (β13), and P462 (β15) are destabilizing hotspots
(Table S2). The folding cooperativity is altered when N175 or P462 are additionally mutated, possibly due
to accumulation of a folding intermediate (Figures S8-S10). These residues form intra-β-barrel
interaction (N415 with L6), or with other SAM complex proteins (P462 with Sam37; S170 with Mdm10),3
and can be functionally relevant. The intrinsic destabilization of N415 affects the stability of the C-
terminal strands during substrate assembly, which is overcome by L6 docking interactions.23 Whether
intrinsic Sam50 destabilization can also promote oligomerization in vivo, remains to be determined.

β-Barrel stability allosterically regulates protein dynamics
Next, we characterize Sam50FL and Sam50Δ120 in PC:PE membranes using all-atom molecular
dynamics (MD) simulations to map the protein’s dynamics (Figures 3, S11-S15). We found larger
spatio-temporal dynamics and conformational states in Sam50FL over Sam50Δ120. This is due to the
intrinsic dynamicity of the POTRA domain, which increases the radius of gyration (R ) (Figures S14-
S15). The root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF) of the TMD is marginally lower in Sam50FL than
Sam50Δ120 (Figures 3a,c, S13a). Particularly, the strand tilt at β1-β3 (w.r.t. bilayer normal) is lower in
Sam50FL than Sam50Δ120, causing structural compaction at the lateral gate in Sam50FL, while Sam50Δ120
β1-β3 are partly open (Figure 3a). Therefore, POTRA may help allosterically modulate the β1-β3 switch
between gate-open and gate-closed conformations.

WF-Sam50Δ120 (W240/F455→A; intrinsically stabilizing residues) showed a broader free energy
landscape (FEL) than Sam50Δ120, due to larger TMD dynamics (Figure S15). Additionally,
W240/F455→A increases the β-barrel midplane and T3 (P218-P234 linking β6-β7) distance by 0.5-1.5 nm
when compared with Sam50Δ120 (Figures 3b-c, S12-S15). Our simulations revealed that this increase in
dynamicity of T3 of only 18 residues –unlike longer loops (L6: 41 residues; L4: 31 residues)– is due to
A240 (on β7) and A455 (on β15) causing an allosteric effect on T3. Hence, the midplane W240 (β7) and
F455 (β15) anchor the TMD, help form structured extramembranous segments, and are vital for Sam50
structural integrity. The loss in membrane anchoring explains the destabilization we observed when
W240 or F455 is replaced (see Figure 2d).

In contrast, SNNP-Sam50Δ120 (S170/N175/N415/P462→A; intrinsically destabilizing residues) shows
a narrow FEL, with an increase in TMD structural order. Here again, T3 dynamicity is high, suggesting
T3 conformational entropy is sensitive to various thermodynamic perturbations in the TMD (Figures 3b-
c, S12-S15). Our simulations establish that the TMD residues of Sam50 exhibit allosteric modulation of
the dynamics of extramembranous regions, and may thereby influence cytosolic Sam35/37 binding, N-
terminal gating, substrate interaction, or Sam50 function.

in nucleating Sam50 folding. Folding is retained in Sam50Δ120, emphasizing the intrinsic ability of the β-
barrel and extramembranous POTRA domains to fold independently.

Trade-off between residues vital for Sam50 folding and function
Our thermodynamics and kinetics measurements identified key residues that cause frustrated
folding, impede rapid β-barrel formation, and affect Sam50 scaffold stability (Figures 2d, 5a-b, S9, S25-
S26)). To assess if these residues were retained evolutionarily for superior function, we examined their
in vivo relevance. We monitored survival of yeast YPH499 sam50::ade2,26 complemented with pFL39-
SAM50FL, pFL39-SAM50Δ120, and their mutants, under non-permissive conditions (37 °C, non-
fermentable carbon source, oxidative stress). We found Sam50 (FL and Δ120) as tolerant to point
mutations (Figure S27). Therefore, we next determined the functional relevance of TMD strands, T3,
and L4/L6, through multiple Xaa→Ala substitutions.

Surprisingly, complementation was successful only for a subset of variants (Figure S27). Non-
permissive mutants mapped to residues at the midplane and cytosolic interface of β10-β14
(L315(β10)/Y390(β12)/T440(β14); K341/V420) (Figure S28). Our in vitro measurements showed that β10
(L315) contributes to mid-β-barrel assembly, and β10-β13 is essential for membrane transfer of L6.
Therefore, we propose that these multiple mutations negatively affect the correct positioning of L6 and
subsequent β15-L6-L7-Sam35 interactions. L315 (β10) is essential in both Sam50FL and Sam50Δ120,
supporting a POTRA-independent functional role for this residue. Others, such as K341 and V420, located
at the neck of L6 and L7, can control loop dynamics and regulate pore size of the Sam50 lumen. T440
can stabilize β15-Sam35 interaction3 at the bilayer interface through vicinal residues (e.g., E437). The
other Sam50 subset that did not support yeast survival included I185(β5)/I277(β8)/G443(β14)→A. We
attributed this to a combined loss in structural features involving T3 (I185) and L4 (I277) dynamics, and
β14 curvature nucleated at G443 (the central hinge residue with unusual ϕ- values; discussed later).
These mutations were lethal also in Sam50FL, and POTRA could not rescue this lethality.

Taken together, residues displaying frustration in Sam50 folding also appear vital for its
biogenesis and its function in the cell. Many of these residues are conserved between BamAEc, Sam50Sc,
and human Sam50 (Figures S29-S30). Our study revealed that, despite the successful evolutionary
divergence of Sam50 for adaptation to the mitochondrial membrane and its interactome in the specific
eukaryotic cell, the retention of select residues from bacteria to humans emphasizes their functional
importance. For example, β14-GT443 is necessary for the hinge-like structural gating motion of Sam50.2,4
Despite causing folding errors, sequences such as β14-β16, or the stereo-selective positioning of
residues such as G443, are retained evolutionarily for their vital role in Sam50 function in vivo.

Cloning, mutant library generation, and protein production
Saccharomyces cerevisiae SAM50 cloned in pGEM4 was a kind gift from Prof. Doron Rapaport
(University of Tübingen, Germany). The complete gene was PCR amplified and re-cloned in pET3a
between NdeI and BamHI, downstream of the T7 promoter. Full-length pET3a–SAM50 was used as the
template for generating the POTRA deleted variant (pET3a–SAM50Δ120). This was achieved through
conventional mutagenesis and gene manipulation, wherein the first 360 nucleotides at the 5′ end of
SAM50 were excised, and the gene re-ligated in-frame to obtain the POTRA–less variant. Both pET3a–
SAM50FL and pET3a–SAM50Δ120 were used as the templates for generating all the mutant variants
described in this study.

The modeled structure of Sam5010 was used as the guide to map residues constituting the
transmembrane domain of this protein. The codon for each non-Ala transmembrane residue of
SAM50Δ120was mutated systematically to Ala using transfer-PCR.S19,43 A total of 165 variants of
Sam50Δ120 were thus generated, and incorporation of the mutation was verified in each case using
Sanger sequencing. Chemically competent Escherichia coli C41 cells were transformed independently
with pET3a–SAM50Δ120 and its 165 mutant variants, and protein expression in the form of inclusion
bodies was achieved upon induction for 4 h with 1 mM (final) isopropyl β-D-thiogalactopyranoside.

Inclusion bodies were extracted and purified (>85% purity) by treatment with 2.75% Triton X-100
followed by 0.5% sodium deoxycholate.14,19,44 The preparations for Sam50Δ120 was additionally
subjected to fast protein liquid chromatography (FPLC) denaturing purification on a 20 mL HiPrep SP-
FF cation ion exchange column using an increasing 1 M NaCl gradient (Buffer B) prepared in 50 mM
acetate buffer pH 5.0 containing 8 M urea (Buffer A). Fractions containing the purest form of Sam50Δ120
were pooled, and dialyzed against water to remove urea, residual buffers, and salts. All protein
preparations (from inclusion bodies and chromatographic purification) were stored at –86 °C as
lyophilized powders. All 166 variants were produced tag-free and without a mitochondrial targeting
sequence(s), and checked for protein integrity on 12% SDS-PAGE before use.

Preparation of large unilamellar vesicles
Lipid vesicles contained the 14-C saturated phosphatidylcholine DMPC (1,2-dimyristoyl-sn-
glycero-3-phosphocholine) doped with a defined concentration (10%) of the 14-C non-lamellar lipid
DMPE (1,2-dimyristoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphoethanolamine). For folding screens, the 16-C
phosphatidylcholine DPPC (1,2-dipalmitoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine) and cholesterol were also
used. Defined molar volumes of DMPC, DMPE, DPPC, and cholesterol, in required ratios and
concentrations, were aliquoted in glass vials. Chloroform, methanol, and trace solvents in the lipid
suspensions were removed by drying under a stream of dry N gas. These lipid films were dried further
2
by lyophilization for 4 h, following which they were stored at –86 °C and used within one week of
preparation.

Lipid resuspension (final concentration = 40 mM) was achieved by hydrating the dried film in
the desired buffer (listed in Table S1), followed by alternating heating–vortexing cycles at 54 °C for 45
min to obtain a suspension of 40 mM lipid. Large unilamellar vesicles (LUVs) of uniform 100 nm
diameter were prepared using 40-50 cycles of extrusion at 35 °C through a 0.1 μm polycarbonate
membrane using the mini-extruder assembly (Avanti Polar Lipids, Inc.).

Preparation of Sam50Δ120 stocks
Different conditions were screened to obtain the buffer, lipid composition, lipid:protein ratios,
temperature, pH, and dilution factor that supported complete folding of Sam50 (details in SI Methods).
125 μM Sam50Δ120 was prepared in 8.0 M GdnHCl in 50 mM citrate buffer pH 5.0 and 10 mM DTT
(unfolded stock). Protein quantification was achieved using a molar extinction coefficient for Sam50Δ120
of 53400 M-1 cm-1 at 280 nm (https://www.expasy.org/resources/protparam). In the first step, this
unfolded protein stock was diluted 10-fold to achieve 12.5 μM Sam50Δ120 in 20 mM LUVs (90 %
DMPC + 10 % DMPE), 50 mM citrate buffer pH 5.0, 4.0 M GdnHCl, and LPR = 1600:1. Next, this
reaction was diluted 5-fold either in buffer (to prepare the folded stock) or 4.0 M GdnHCl (to prepare
the unfolded stock). Both stock preparations were incubated for 12-14 h at 28 °C, with rotational
mixing. These folded and unfolded stocks contained final concentrations of 2.5 µM protein, 4 mM
LUVs (90 % DMPC + 10 % DMPE), 50 mM citrate buffer pH 5.0, 0.2 mM DTT, and 0.8 M GdnHCl
(folded stock) or 4.0 M GdnHCl (unfolded stock). The final LPR was 1600:1. These preparations were
diluted an additional 6-fold in the equilibrium thermodynamics and kinetics experiments. This stepwise
protocol was also followed for the preparation of Sam50FL.

Pulse proteolysis
Unlike bacterial outer membrane proteins, Sam50Δ120 does not exhibit differential mobility on
cold SDS-PAGE. Therefore, to assess folding efficiency, the folded protein stock prepared as described
above, was subjected to proteolysis using the robust protease proteinase K (PK).45 Protein stocks were
diluted with 50 mM citrate buffer pH 5.0 and PK was diluted in PK buffer. PK was added so as to
achieve different protein:PK ratio (5:1 and 1:3.5) in the final reaction. Samples were drawn at different
time intervals and the reaction quenched by addition of phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride (final
concentration = 8 mM or 1.2 mM). Samples were loaded on 12% SDS-PAGE and checked for protease
protection, by comparing with the appropriate controls (Figures 1c, S1b).

Far-UV circular dichroism (CD) measurements
The secondary structure content of the folded protein was assessed on a JASCO J-815 far-UV
CD spectropolarimeter (JASCO Inc., Japan). The folded stock protein (2.5 μM protein folded in 4 mM
LUVs) was subjected to wavelength scans from 210–260 nm at 1 nm increments and scan speed of 50
nm/min, at 28 °C, using a quartz cuvette of 1 mm path length. The contribution from buffer, GdnHCl
and lipid were nullified using appropriate blank corrections, and the raw ellipticity values were
smoothened using the means–movement method.45 The averaged raw ellipticity (θ, mdeg) from three
accumulations was converted to molar ellipticity (ME) at each wavelength,19 and plotted (Figure 1d).
Per-residue ellipticity was calculated by dividing the ME at each wavelength by the total number of
residues. The signal at ~255-260 nm was set to 0 mdeg, to nullify effects of scattering from LUV
preparations and plotted as normalized θ (mdeg) for the mutants (Figure S6).

Transmission electron microscopy
To check the integrity and size of vesicles, TEM images were obtained. Protein-free vesicles
(0.5 mg/ml) recovered after rotational mixing (similar to the stock preparations) at 1100 rpm for 14 h at
28 °C, were immobilized by coating on a carbon–coated copper grid, followed by staining with 2%
uranyl acetate, washing with milliQ, and drying at 28 °C for 4 h. TEM images were obtained on a
ThermoFisher Scientific TalosTM F200S (S)TEM operated at accelerated voltage of 200 kV at –196 °C.

Electrophysiology measurements
Sam50 is a β-barrel with a central luminal pore with a sufficiently large diameter to facilitate the
movement of ions. We used this feature of the protein to check if Sam50Δ120 can form a complete
functional β-barrel without its soluble N-terminal POTRA domain. To study the channel forming

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
regulation of the  OMPs is an important and long-standing question. Ravi and his/her colleagues investigated the
thermodynamic and kinetics of an N-terminus truncated Sam50 (Sam50 1-120) variants in the lipid bilayer environment to
exhibit their thermodynamic stability, path-independent folding, and stepwise β-barrel assembly process. The study offers
insights into how Sam50’s folding process is regulated by its β-strands and loops, although interesting, no external factors,
such as the SAM complex, were considered in this analysis. More comprehensive investigations, such as those including
the SAM complex, would be necessary to gain a more complete understanding of Sam50’s folding dynamics. While the
authors have made significant strides in mapping key residues involved in Sam50 folding, these results may not fully
address the broader  OMP-folding-regulation mechanism. Additionally, the manuscript’s writing expression could be
improved to enhance clarity and ensure broader accessibility to the findings. A thorough revision of the manuscript is
recommended to improve readability. Below are some detailed suggestions for improvement:
Major:
1. Previous findings support that the assembly of the  OMP needs the help of the SAM/BAM machine. Ravi et al. found that
the Sam50 can spontaneously insert the N-terminal strands into the membrane, even without the association of the SAM
complex. The author should provide more interpretations for this very unexpected finding.
2. Why must the authors use the Sam50 1-120 rather than a full-length Sam50? I would like to know if they can get similar
results when they use FL-Sam50 as a target, as well as the Tom40 or Mdm10.
3. Page 4 line 16, a fully folded  OMP may be exhibited by a crosslinking strategy (Qiu, Jian et al. Cell. 2013 Aug
1;154(3):596-608. doi: 10.1016/j.cell.2013.06.033.). Considering there is no SAM complex in the LUV, the author should
provide evidence showing that this spontaneous insertion system really works.
4. Mammalian Sam50 is related to the neurological disease in mammals rather than the fungal Sam50. Also, the Mdm10 is
just a potential linker in the fungal; there are currently no homologs of Mdm10 in human cells. So, the authors should
carefully present the sentence in the abstract: “Our findings thus show how conformational buffering of Sam50 structure-
function handles evolved for superior mito-biogenesis and mito-ER interactome and pave the way for designing knowledge-
based peptide therapeutics for neurological ailments.”
5. The model is confusing. 1) The evidence for proving the beta-strand self-folding when binding the small Tim chaperone
needs to be more characterized. 2) The Step 3 presented here is involved in the hybrid of the nascent beta-strand and the
template beta-strand. This step may represent a key process for understanding the beta-OPM folding, but details are absent
in the zoom-in figures. 3) The thermodynamics and kinetics measurements in the paper did not contain SAM complex.
Although the authors have included an in vivo relevance for some chosen Sam50 variants, they’d better only provide this
model figure just to show the spontaneous folding process of Sam50.
6. The POTRA domain is a conserved part in the 16-beta-strands OMPs, such as BamA in bacteria and OPE80 in
chloroplast. The function of the POTRA domain is currently elusive. Could the authors figure out some interpretation for the
function of the POTRA domain from the data and analysis in Figure 3? Also, could the authors give some speculations as to
why different 16-beta-strands OMPs chose different numbers of POTRA domain?
Minor:
1. Page 4, lines 15, 31, 32, and 36, It is not clear about the difference between the “path-independent assembly” and the
“path-dependent assembly”. The authors should add some definitions of the two types of assembly.
2. Fig 1g, what’s the difference between the control and the FL? It seems like the same construct but with a different
phenotype in some situations.
3. Fig 1f, the authors should include a negative control such as a liposome without protein.
4. Figure 1c. The author did not label the band, which would confuse them. Additionally, the accumulation of the ~27 kDa
species cannot be observed clearly (lane 5). Furthermore, the folded Sam50 should not be digested by PK without PMSF
(lane 6).
5. Figure 3b. This MDS should be further confirmed by a single molecular experiment, for instance, smFRET.
6. Page 9 line 11, are the conserved residues in BamAEc or other beta-OMPs also involved in their folding regulation?

7. Figure 3a, the results relevant to the all-atom MDS of Sam50 120 and full-length Sam50 are not clear. The author should

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Referee report for Ravi et al: In this paper, the authors present a series of biophysical and biochemical assays and
simulations characterizing the folding and stability of the Sam50 protein in model membranes. They further perform in vivo
assays in yeast to assess lethal sets of residue mutations. The introduction establishes that this mitochondrial membrane
protein is essential for cells and notes that defects in its function contribute to mitochondrial disorders. Overall, the authors
have collected large datasets to comprehensively assess single-point residue mutations (none of which are lethal), some
‘multipoint’ mutations, as well as assays that identify folding transition states. While these datasets will be useful to
researchers studying the protein Sam50, the paper is extremely technical and does not establish a clear or coherent story
about how all of this data is broadly useful or insightful to non-experts or a broad audience in biology or biophysics, or how it
will be useful for therapeutics or disease. A persistent issue is the use of words that are not standard in biophysics or are
misused, along with statements that do not make sense. There are many aspects of the system that are not clear even after
reading the paper several times. For example, is the folding ever studied in the membrane in the presence of the SAM
chaperone? Is it the Sam50 dimer (Sam50b and Sam50a)? Or just one subunit? A major issue is that the collected results
are not integrated together. The MD simulations in particular are almost completely divorced from the study of folding of the
protein, as they only compare energy landscapes of structures under mutations, showing rather minor effects. Many of the
figures do not support strong conclusions (Fig 3 and 4), and I am not sure if Fig 5 is speculation or data.
General issues:
The abstract is already very difficult to parse. What does ‘regulators’ mean? MDS is not a standard acronym, even MD would
be better. 165 variants of Sam50 is actually 165 mutations to the Sam50b subunit? Multipoint is not a familiar or standard
word in biophysics: at multiple residues in the sequence. I am not sure why the word mutation is rarely used. ‘This
metastable structure’? Which metastable structure is this referring to? And again, what are ‘microscopic regulators’? What is
conformational buffering? What are structure-function handles?
In short, the authors do not seem to be entirely clear what they are trying to say, and have leaned on broad generalizations
that muddy what approach they have taken and what they have learned. The word regulators needs to be replaced with
something specific, like residues, secondary structures, or something that reflects what they tested and learned.
These sentences contain more information: “We show that Sam50 folds through multipoint nucleation and N-terminal
structuring, whereas C-terminal frustrated folding forms kinetically-trapped intermediates. This unexpected folding correlates
mechanistically with SAM-assisted in vivo assembly”. However they are still confusing. When does the C-terminal folding
occur, do they see this in the membrane? The fact that this is even undergoing folding in the membrane is not clear, nor is it
clear that they look at only one subunit, or that the SAM machinery is known to assist in protein folding within membranes.
The authors describe the structure as “metastable” throughout the text. This has a strict thermodynamic meaning: this
structure is not the free energy minimum, but can persist for some time range because it has a barrier separating it from the
free energy minimum. This is therefore not the most favorable equilibrium structure. When do they show this? It appears to
be asserted without support. They seem to be abusing the word metastable, or at least haven’t actually provided evidence in
the text of the metastability. To the contrary, that the protein folds to a functional state on its own despite many mutations
seems to indicate overall stability.
The MD simulation results are largely divorced from the rest of the study. Despite having extensive residue-level
experimental data, the simulations are not directly compared to the experiments in any way. The main conclusion is that the
free energy landscape becomes wider as a function of the RMSD, but they already showed that that protein has a wider
RMSD because it has an extra domain, so it will automatically sample more values. These are not insightful plots about the
function. They have a proposed folding mechanism and it is not interrogated using the atomistic simulations.
The authors refer to a ‘kinetic free energy’ (P7L4) and ‘energetic contributions from both kinetic and thermodynamic
components’ (P10L31). This is misleading. Free energies are by definition equilibrium measurements that have no kinetic
component. If they extracted them from experiments that also measured kinetics, that is fine, but don’t assign this confusing
language to a free energy.
The following specific parts in the manuscript require further clarification and/or restructuring:
On page 3 it is mentioned that the SAM complex helps to fold Sam50. However, all of the results seem to be Sam50 folding
by itself in the membrane, rather than folding with the assistance of the SAM chaperone activity.
Figure 4: I am not sure how to interpret these plots, they seem more like supplementary information. There are a series of
points and lines, and what I am supposed to expect vs what they see is not clear from the plot. Comparison of (d) and (e)
requires staring at these sequences and picking out variations, none of which are highlighted and made clear. Yes there are
differences between them, what do I learn from this?
Figure 5: Are these results or speculation? Where did the Tims come from? These proteins were never mentioned and were
not included in the experiments.
Page 3: what do the superscripts mean on the names of proteins? Some are Sam50, one is SAM, why?
P4 L38: Protein folding is bimolecular? What does this mean? Bimolecular reactions typically refer to two species at well-
mixed concentrations binding to one another through space. Folding is a polymer dynamics problem. At no point in the SI
does it show a bimolecular treatment of the observed dynamics. Sums of exponentials are not indicative of a bimolecular
reaction (which has units of M-1s-1 for rates).
P5 L5: Surface area in units of kcal /mol /M, this is completely unfamiliar to non-experts
Fig 3a overlaid structures are very difficult to understand. What are we supposed to be seeing here?
Fig 3d: what do we learn from these plots? It is unsurprising that FE landscape is broader with respect to RMSD when
there’s a large domain added that increases the RMSD.
Fig 3d D120 landscape: are those two bumps supposed to be the metastable and stable states?
Fig 3c: Are these curves statistically significantly different? Error shading?
Statements that are unclear and are not supported by data:
'Beta barrel stability allosterically regulates protein dynamics'? How does ‘stability’ allosterically regulate dynamics? I have
no idea what this is trying to say.
P6 L22: “Our simulations establish how intrinsically destabilizing residues modulate signal propagation across the
membrane, with zonal changes (cytosolic Sam35/37 binding, N-terminal gating, substrate interaction) allosterically
propagating through the β-barrel, to alter IMS dynamics and regulate Sam50 function”. What are zonal changes? Again the

Why do the authors fit to a triple exponential for folding and a double exponential for unfolding? Where did this choice for the
number of rates come from?
S19: Why do the kinetics and equilibrium measurements overlay so well (“excellent overlay”) when at the same time,
“Sam50Δ120 undergoes slow rearrangement (possibly through multiple pathways of near-equal populations), which cannot
be captured in the rapid kinetics measurements, but is evident in the equilibrium titrations.”?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This manuscript by Ravi et al. presents a detailed and multifaceted investigation into the folding mechanism, stability, and
functional regulation of the mitochondrial outer membrane protein Sam50. By integrating thermodynamic profiling,
ultrafast folding kinetics, molecular dynamics simulations, and in vivo functional assays, the authors provide detailed insights into the
folding landscape and structure-function relationships of Sam50.
This study addresses a significant gap in our understanding of mitochondrial β-barrel assembly. Major Strengths include the
comprehensive approach combining experimental and computational tools. Also, the mapping of thermodynamically
(de)stabilizing hotspots and their in vivo validation enhances the translational relevance of the work. I have a few points that
need to be addressed before considering publication.
The folding studies were performed in a PC:PE (90:10) lipid system. While this is experimentally tractable, it doesn't fully
mimic the native mitochondrial outer membrane environment. The authors mention the use of "native-like" conditions, but
this lipid mixture is distinct from actual mitochondrial membranes. The manuscript would benefit from a discussion on how
the choice of lipid composition may influence Sam50 folding energetics and the generalizability of the findings to in vivo
conditions.
The manuscript notes the potential for structure-based peptidotherapeutic development. However, this important point is not
developed in detail. The authors should elaborate on which structural or energetic features of Sam50 could be rationally
targeted for therapeutic design and how their findings might inform future efforts. As it stands, the therapeutic implications are
speculative without further context.
The figure captions are too long and include large amounts of methodological and interpretive information, which would be
better placed in the main text. The paper would benefit from concise captions and improved integration of the relevant details
into the Results and Discussion sections.
Minor points:
Page 5: I didn't understand the units of surface area ("3.01 kcal/mol*M"). Can the authors clarify?
Page 5: "other transmembrane Phe(18), Tyr(6), and Trp(3), do not stabilize the..." - maybe say residues after Phe, Tyr, and
Trp?
Page 12: "evisage" - should be envision
Page 12: "drug designing" - should be design

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
Ravi et al have addressed a part of my concerns. This study offers insights into how Sam50’s folding process is regulated by its β-strands and loops. The additional revisions have strengthened the manuscript; however, despite the authors' efforts to address the reviewers' comments, some aspects still require further clarification. Given that it is the first time showing that Sam50 can fold successfully in membranes in an in vitro system, without assistance from the SAM complex, the authors should provide more compelling evidence showing that this spontaneous insertion system works (see below). Moreover, they should better interpret whether this spontaneous insertion process could occur in the mitochondrial outer membrane under physiological conditions.
Major:
1. Although the authors showed four results that tried to prove the Sam501-120 can be spontaneously inserted into the
artificial membrane, there are also things that need to be validated.
a)Figure 1c. The folded/unfolded Sam50Δ1–120 cannot be digested by proteinase K in the presence of PMSF, since PMSF should fully inhibit PK. As the 27-kDa band appears under similar conditions in Figure S1b, the authors should show this digestion result in Figure 1c without PMSF to clarify this point.
b)Figure 1d. I suggest separating the two datasets in Figure 1d into two individual panels to enhance readability.
c)Figure 1f. From the perspective of experimental completeness, a protein-free planar bilayer membrane should be included as a negative control in the electrophysiological recordings, even if no current is expected. This would help confirm that any observed current is indeed attributable to Sam50.
d)The electrophysiological experiment is intended to demonstrate that the refolded Sam50 is functional. However, ScSam50 has not been reported to act as an ion channel. Therefore, additional evidence is needed to confirm that Sam50 was fully folded in the authors’ system. Alternative functional assays or structural confirmation would be helpful.
2. The folding behavior of β-OMPs in artificial membranes may not reflect their folding in mitochondrial outer membranes.
Given that Sam50 is essential for yeast viability (Paschen et al., Nature, 2003; Kozjak et al., J Biol Chem, 2003; Gentle et al.,
J Cell Biol, 2004), the authors should discuss whether β-OMPs can spontaneously fold in mitochondria in the absence of the
SAM complex. Furthermore, the discussion should be expanded to include other β-OMPs mentioned in the rebuttal letter,
such as Tom40 and VDACs.
3. In the rebuttal letter, the authors mention three cryo-EM studies that captured the SAM complex “in action” — with fully
captured Mdm10, fully folded Tom40, and partially folded Tom40. However, in Figure 6 (panel “2”), only the interaction
residues of “SNNP” within the SAM and SAM–Mdm10 structures are mapped. The authors should also address: 1) The
“SNNP” motif in the two SAM–Tom40 structures. 2) The corresponding residues in the AlphaFold-predicted
SAM–Porin complex.
Minor:
1. Figure 6, the author should use “a, b, c” as icons rather than “1, 2, 3”.
2. Throughout the manuscript, replace “mOMP” with the more widely accepted term “β-OMP.
3. The term “insertase” is used to describe Sam50 in the revised version. However, this term is typically reserved for
YidC/Alb3/Oxa1 family proteins, which mediate the insertion and folding of α-helical membrane proteins. The authors should
reconsider this terminology or provide justification for its use in this context.
4. The role of the POTRA domain should be discussed more thoroughly in the Discussion section.
5. The English language in the manuscript remains awkward in places and sometimes difficult to follow. Careful
proofreading and editing are needed to improve the clarity, flow, and overall readability of the text.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors have significantly improved the text through rewriting their manuscript, with more precise language, improved integration of the distinct parts into a coherent narrative, and improved figure clarity. Additionally, they have clarified many of the details and confusing language. However, we still have issues that we feel should be addressed:
1. Regarding the electrophysiology experiments:
a. While it’s clear that the properly folded Sam50 forms a membrane channel, it is not established how a channel current and conductance switching would be indicative of “full functionality” as claimed in the electrophysiology results.
b. The characterization in the text of the data in fig 1f seems off: the text says both FL and d120 have reduction from ~2-3 to ~1 nS at >+-50mV. Figure 1f shows a change from above 3 to below 3 nS for d120 rather inconsistently with applied voltage, appearing briefly for descending voltage >~200mV, and again for increasing negative voltage from around -400mV to nearly 0. The FL is similar, but with conductance uniformly lower by ~1nS. Additionally, the d120 variant appears to have a third conductance state not seen in the FL trace.
c. Overall, these data seem not to contribute much to the rest of the (very detailed) study of the folding and structure of
Sam50.
2. Regarding the molecular dynamics simulations:
a. The first paragraph of the section “β-Barrel stability allosterically regulates protein dynamics” concludes that “POTRA can regulate gate dynamics, and may drive the β1-β3 switch…” This might match the more classical definition of allostery, but it’s difficult to understand how β-barrel stability regulating gate dynamics would be considered allostery.
b. Our prior comment on error shading in fig 3c seems to have been misinterpreted; it should be possible to show the error
on the mean for the RMSF curves in 3c, e.g. by bootstrapping, so that one can see to what extent the different portions of the
curves are different within statistical error.
c. Caption of 3b says that FL to d120 results in a decrease in T3 “dynamicity” by >1nm. I would think dynamicity would relate to changes or fluctuations. Neither of those two traces show much dynamicity, the change from FL to d120 just shows a change in a rather static distance.
d. Fig 3c: The emphasis on turn 3 seems to show that while FL and d120 do not fluctuate much here, the two mutants do,
which agrees with the result of 3b. Loop 4 seems to be shown as a counter example where no change occurs in mutants.
This could be made more clear in the figure/legend.
e. Fig 3e is still not informative. How do these FEL connect to the point about conformational gate opening/closing. They
report ‘a broader FEL’ in WF-d120. Despite a FEL directly reporting on the relative probability of sampled configurations,
they are not used in this way. The color bars also do not seem to agree with the labels on the z-axis, where d120 reaches
9kJ/mol by eye, but is colored orange. If the FEL is not a main point, as the authors acknowledged in their response, then
why are they being shown in the main text?
3. In the author's response, they state “Yes, by and large, free energies are equilibrium measurements. However, for
membrane proteins, it has been demonstrated through several studies that kinetic components also contribute to the
measured free energy”. This suggests a misunderstanding of what free energy is. We are not arguing that kinetic trapping
cannot occur in protein folding, nor that this can impact how measurements report on the probability of sampled states.
However, do not refer to it as a free energy when that is defined only for an equilibrium ensemble. If kinetic (time-dependent)
elements impact the measured distribution of sampled states, then one is not measuring a free energy. This is non-negotiable. When the authors abuse precise, thermodynamic terminology, it undermines the study. Free energies are by definition controlled entirely by the Boltzmann distribution, and not by any time-dependent factors. The reworded statement does now avoid making this assertion. However, one could argue that there is no need to use the word ‘kinetic stability’,
when kinetic or time-dependent on its own will suffice, although this is not an essential change. If hysteresis occurs, this
cannot be an equilibrium transition between states, as equilibrium transitions are not dependent on paths/history. Or at least
the measurements are not capable of sampling the equilibrium transitions.
a. In the SI, it is remarked that the kinetic free energy is “deduced” from fits to SI equation 6, which does not contain that
variable on its own. Is it defined from the ratio kU/kF being taken equal to an effective folding dissociation constant?
4. We appreciate that the authors removed the word metastable. Despite this modification the authors insist in their response
that “we disagree with the Reviewer’s comment that a metastable state is unfavorable”. It is by its very definition not the free
energy minimum, which means that it is indeed unfavorable relative to the thermodynamic free energy minimum. This is
true whether it is metastable in state space (i.e. a metastable liquid relative to a solid) or metastable within a free energy
landscape of an equilibrium ensemble, where a higher energy minimum is metastable because of barriers separating it from
neighboring states. This minimum on the FEL can only be termed metastable if it is not the global free energy minimum.
5. Fig 4b and text say that unfolding rates were obtained from interpolation, which seems to be taking the value of the linear
fit at a particular concentration of GdnHCl (5.5M and 4.5M). Why those specific concentrations?
6. Fig S31 is a helpful illustration of the kinetic model of folding in LUVs that plays a central role in the paper; the authors
might consider having this as part of figure 4, where the folding and unfolding rate measurements are shown. Also regarding
Fig S31: There are rates for folding to the transition states, and unfolding from the final structure to the transition states, but
not for folding from transition states to final state. Where are the rates that connect the transition state to the folded state?
How do they know that the unfolding from the folded state returns them to the transition state and not to the previous
intermediate or the disordered/adsorbed state?
7. Fig 6 caption says G443→A is not tolerated and causes loss in cell viability, but wasn’t it established earlier that no single
point substitutions resulted in loss of cell viability?
8. In the referee response, they state “The proposed folding mechanism derived from kinetics measurements is distinct from
the dynamics we obtain for the post-folded structure in our MD simulations, and there is nothing to interrogate in this.” How is
there nothing to interrogate when they seem to be stating that the simulations are in disagreement with the experimental
measurements?

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Manuscript reference number: NCOMMS-25-06253-T
Revised Title: Linking multipoint folding and stability with functional regulation in the
mitochondrial outer membrane protein insertase.
We thank the editor and the Reviewers for their time and for the opportunity to resubmit our
work. We present our extensively revised manuscript in line with the Reviewers’ suggestions.
We take this opportunity to emphasize the importance of our findings. Several studies
exist on how soluble proteins fold, which, combined with their structures, have together led to de
novo design of these molecules. Studies on membrane protein folding, particularly the β-barrels,
however, are extremely limited. Here again, information is available only for the bacterial
proteins. Thus far, no study has attempted to map the precise processes involved in the
stepwise folding of any eukaryotic β-barrel. Ours is the first to report it.
We acknowledge that our work involves artificial membranes and non-native conditions.
Yet, studies have consistently demonstrated how invaluable in vitro findings remain for
membrane proteins, and we present three such recent examples involving OMPs:
1. Protein-lipid charge interactions control the folding of outer membrane proteins into
asymmetric membranes. Nat Chem 2023 15(12):1754-1764.
2. The translocation assembly module (TAM) catalyzes the assembly of bacterial outer
membrane proteins in vitro. Nat Commun 2024 15(1):7246.
3. Conformational plasticity of mitochondrial VDAC2 controls the kinetics of its interaction with
cytosolic proteins. Sci Adv 2025 11(17):eadv4410.
An in vitro biophysical characterization is done with a specific purpose: here, we draw
parallels between the mechanisms we capture for Sam50 folding and stability, to that
hypothesized to occur in the cell. Our study maps the folding events of Sam50 using the widely
accepted Φ-value analysis. The advantage of our approach is providing structures of the
intermediates that are not possible to capture in vivo, despite the currently available
technologies. We have additionally correlated folding events with the stability of this protein and
linked it to cell survival. With this, we obtained new insights into why Sam50 exhibits specific
biochemical traits. Three such major findings are:
1. Sam50 structurally interconverts between “gate-closed” and “gate-open” states. We now
show how this transition occurs, and provide a molecular and energetic basis for it.
2. There are only three cryo-EM studies thus far which could capture the SAM complex “in
action” – two with fully folded Mdm10 (Takeda et a., Nature 2021), and Tom40 (Wang et al.,
Science 2021), and one with a partially folded Tom40 (Takeda et al., Nat. Struct. Mol. Biol.
2023). No study has captured how Sam50 itself folds. Ours is the first.
3. We prove –for the very first time– that Sam50 can fold successfully in membranes, without
assistance from SAM complex. We also identify how Sam50 possesses regions that are a
bottleneck for self-assembly: the C-terminal strands that form non-native interactions.
All scientific approaches have their limitations and demand deviation from true in vivo –
be it fluorophore labeling, cryoEM samples, modified cell lines, mouse models for human
systems– immediately rendering them non-native. Given how no one has attempted to study the
folding of this very essential mitochondrial protein, we hope that you would appreciate the
magnitude of our efforts, the breakthrough we have achieved in mapping the stepwise assembly
of Sam50, identifying stabilizing elements, and linking both Sam50 thermodynamics and kinetics
with its function in vivo, and accept our study in Nature Communications.
Response page 1
Reviewers' comments and Author responses:
In this response file, the Reviewers’ comments are in blue, and our responses, in black.
Wherever substantial changes were made in line with the Reviewer’s comments, we present the
revised text as-is for your ready reference, along with our response.
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
Regulation of the bOMPs is an important and long-standing question. Ravi and his/her
colleagues investigated the thermodynamic and kinetics of an N-terminus truncated Sam50
(Sam50D1-120) variants in the lipid bilayer environment to exhibit their thermodynamic stability,
path-independent folding, and stepwise β-barrel assembly process. The study offers insights
into how Sam50’s folding process is regulated by its β-strands and loops, although interesting,
no external factors, such as the SAM complex, were considered in this analysis. More
comprehensive investigations, such as those including the SAM complex, would be necessary
to gain a more complete understanding of Sam50’s folding dynamics.
Author response: We thank the reviewer for appreciating our work and for sharing the
suggestions. We specifically chose our study on Sam50 without its auxiliary factors, so that we
can successfully map the step-wise folding events of this protein, and identify residues that are
vital for its stability and function. Our aim here is to obtain precise insights into the regulatory
elements, which would be extremely difficult to accurately determine if this protein were present
as a complex. We finally propose how our findings link to in vivo events. To clarify that we are
studying only Sam50, we have now added this sentence in the Introduction (page 3, lines 29-
31):
We show that Sam50 TMD folds and functions independent of its POTRA
domain, SAM complex, and Sam35/37.
We are certain that our findings will pave the way for a more comprehensive understanding of
SAM complex assembly in vivo.
While the authors have made significant strides in mapping key residues involved in Sam50
folding, these results may not fully address the broader bOMP-folding-regulation mechanism.
Author response: We understand the Reviewer’s skepticism. However, studies on β-barrel
mOMPs are extremely limited, and only three structures are presently available that provide
snapshots of how these proteins assemble. Furthermore, while end-state structures can still be
predicted for β-barrel mOMPs through AI tools, how this structure is achieved is still unsolved for
membrane proteins in general, and mOMPs in particular. To this end, our current study aims to
bridge this immense void in our understanding of mOMP folding-function-regulation mechanism,
by obtaining detailed information at the residue-level for the mitochondrial Sam50 β-barrel. We
use tools and approaches well-established for soluble proteins, to understand stepwise events
in Sam50 folding, stability of the folded structure, and how both energetic contributions link to
the function of this protein. We are confident that our study will inspire broader research on
many other vital OMPs.
Additionally, the manuscript’s writing expression could be improved to enhance clarity and
ensure broader accessibility to the findings. A thorough revision of the manuscript is
recommended to improve readability.
Author response: We welcome the suggestion, and apologize that the earlier submission was
more technical. We have now revised the manuscript extensively to retain a clear storyline with
broader accessibility and clarity.
Response page 2
Below are some detailed suggestions for improvement:
Major:
1. Previous findings support that the assembly of the OMP needs the help of the SAM/BAM
machine. Ravi et al. found that the Sam50 can spontaneously insert the N-terminal strands into
the membrane, even without the association of the SAM complex. The author should provide
more interpretations for this very unexpected finding.
Author response: We welcome the suggestion. In fact, a similar assumption was made for
bacterial β-barrels, that they could only be assembled correctly by the BAM complex. SAM-
independent unassisted folding of other mitochondrial OMPs (including yeast Por1, mouse
VDAC1, and the three human VDACs 1/2/3) have been demonstrated in artificial detergents,
bicelles, and vesicles. Hence, our finding that Sam50 can fold without the help of SAM/BAM is
not unexpected. As suggested by the Reviewer, we now include a statement to this effect on
page 4, lines 9-11, with the relevant citations:
As seen with BamA11 and other mOMPs,12,13 Sam50 (FL and Δ120) can fold
spontaneously in artificial membranes without SAM assistance.
2. Why must the authors use the Sam501-120 rather than a full-length Sam50? I would like to
know if they can get similar results when they use FL-Sam50 as a target, as well as the Tom40
or Mdm10.
Author response: Earlier studies indicate that the POTRA domain is redundant, and non-
essential for Sam50 function (Cell 2008 132(6):1011-24). Given how we intended to understand
the folding and stability of Sam50 without any auxiliary factors, we reasoned that POTRA would
also be an auxiliary factor. Removing the soluble POTRA domain will decrease any interference
in our measurements from the extramembranous region, thereby helping us to precisely
interpret the role of transmembrane residues in the folding of Sam50. We have succinctly
justified our approach on page 4, lines 5-7:
We asked if the TMD was sufficient for Sam50 folding, stability, and function. To
address this, we generated a POTRA-less variant of yeast Sam50 […]
Other studies from our lab on Sam50FL, human Tom40, human VDAC2, and bacterial BamA
reveal multiple folding pathways for each protein. Some show unique assembly mechanisms,
while others are similar to the Sam50Δ120 pathways we report here. These findings are currently
in different stages of being published (under review, under revision). We have not worked on
Mdm10 (since it is present only in mitochondria of lower eukaryotes, and absent in human
mitochondria), but we hypothesize that spontaneous membrane insertion and path-independent
folding are features that this mOMP also possesses.
3. Page 4 line 16, a fully folded OMP may be exhibited by a crosslinking strategy (Qiu, Jian et
al. Cell. 2013 Aug 1;154(3):596-608. doi: 10.1016/j.cell.2013.06.033.). Considering there is no
SAM complex in the LUV, the author should provide evidence showing that this spontaneous
insertion system really works.
Author response: We agree that cross-linking is one strategy to confirm folding. While this is a
good approach in vivo, this does not necessarily guarantee that other parts of the β-barrel are
definitely folded in vitro. In our experiments, to confirm that Sam50 indeed folds spontaneously,
we used four different experimental approaches that could be tested simultaneously on Sam50-
FL, Sam50-Δ120, or any of the Ala variants:
1. Resistance to proteolysis by a robust non-specific protease such as proteinase K
(Figure 1c). Here, an unfolded/ membrane-adsorbed/ partially folded protein is rapidly digested
by proteinase K (shown in the same gel).
Response page 3
2. β-Rich secondary structure content confirmed using far-UV circular dichroism (CD)
spectropolarimetry (Figure 1d). The structural content is comparable to reported
ellipticity values for another 16-stranded bacterial β-barrel.
3. Change in Trp fluorescence intensity (2-fold increase) and emission maxima (10-nm
blue-shifted emission) (Figure 1d, inset).
4. Single-channel electrophysiology of these artificially folded samples shows gating
characteristics that match previous reports which studied reconstituted SAM complex
(Figure 1f).
Put together, these results (described on page 4, lines 14-28, and Figure 1) confirm that the
Sam50 proteins we are characterizing do indeed fold and achieve a functionally competent
state.
4. Mammalian Sam50 is related to the neurological disease in mammals rather than the fungal
Sam50. Also, the Mdm10 is just a potential linker in the fungal; there are currently no homologs
of Mdm10 in human cells. So, the authors should carefully present the sentence in the abstract:
“Our findings thus show how conformational buffering of Sam50 structure-
function handles evolved for superior mito-biogenesis and mito-ER interactome and pave the way for designing knowledge-
based peptide therapeutics for neurological ailments.”
Author response: We agree with the Reviewer. Hence, we have reworded the abstract and the
conclusion sections as follows:
Abstract (page 2, lines 14-17):
Our findings suggest how the dynamic structure of Sam50 offers a functional
advantage in vivo, with selective residues that affect the folding, stability, and
function, correlating directly with the protein’s sensitivity to mutations.
Conclusions (page 11, lines 34-38):
The Sam50 destabilization we detect upon mutation of key residues can
substantially alter SAM complex function, affecting mitochondrial health. The
identification of residues tailored for stability and functional efficacy for vital
proteins, such as what we report for Sam50, can unveil mechanistic correlations
of mOMPs under both health and disease states, furthering the design of possible
therapeutic molecules.
5. The model is confusing.
Author response: We have now simplified the model we present. We have divided the figure
into three segments in Figure 6:
Scheme 1 provides what we have mapped from our -value analysis.
Scheme 2 illustrates residues we identify as essential for Sam50, and how it
relates to the important interactions that these residues establish (derived from
previously reported structures).
Scheme 3 focuses specifically on the functional importance of the intrinsically
destabilized β4-β6 we identify, on the conformational interconversion Sam50
undergoes. The figure also illustrates the importance of β14-G443.
1) The evidence for proving the beta-strand self-folding when binding the small Tim chaperone
needs to be more characterized.
Author response: We have now edited this figure to only reflect our observations from our
experiments. The illustration involving small Tim chaperons has now been removed.
2) The Step 3 presented here is involved in the hybrid of the nascent beta-strand and the
template beta-strand. This step may represent a key process for understanding the beta-OPM
folding, but details are absent in the zoom-in figures.
Response page 4
Author response: Since this information was not obtained directly from our experiments, we
have now removed it from the main figure. However, we agree with the Reviewer that this hybrid
barrel formation is a key step in mOMP insertion in vivo. Hence, we have moved this figure to
the supplementary information (now Figure S32), and included a zoomed-in image of Step 3.
3) The thermodynamics and kinetics measurements in the paper did not contain SAM complex.
Although the authors have included an in vivo relevance for some chosen Sam50 variants,
they’d better only provide this model figure just to show the spontaneous folding process of
Sam50.
Author response: We agree. We have removed all reference to the SAM complex in this figure,
and have now shown only the unassisted assembly mechanism of Sam50 that we map from our
study.
6. The POTRA domain is a conserved part in the 16-beta-strands OMPs, such as BamA in
bacteria and OPE80 in chloroplast. The function of the POTRA domain is currently elusive.
Could the authors figure out some interpretation for the function of the POTRA domain from the
data and analysis in Figure 3? Also, could the authors give some speculations as to
why different 16-beta-strands OMPs chose different numbers of POTRA domain?
Author response: The question on Figure 3 is a very interesting one! Our in vitro
measurements (Figure 1c-f) suggest that POTRA is likely a redundant feature of yeast Sam50.
We see no measurable difference in yeast survival under permissive and non-permissive growth
conditions, despite POTRA deletion (Figure 1g). Hence, this change appears well-tolerated by
the cell. Our conclusion is supported by a previous study (Cell 2008 132(6):1011-24). However,
from our MD simulations (Figure 3), we find that the presence of POTRA structurally compacts
the transmembrane domain by altering the strand tilt angle, particularly at β1-β3. We believe
that this may alter the efficiency with which the transmembrane domain transitions between
“gate-closed” and “gate-open” states, thereby influencing the binding and/or release of a
precursor protein in mitochondria. A previous study also suggests that POTRA may play a role
in precursor release (Mol Biol Cell 2011 22(16):2823-33). Putting together our observations,
we
have now proposed the following in our revised manuscript (page 5, lines 37-40):
Particularly, the strand tilt at β1-β3 (w.r.t. bilayer normal) is lower in Sam50FL
than Sam50Δ120, causing structural compaction at the lateral gate in Sam50FL,
while Sam50Δ120 β1-β3 is partly open (Figure 3a). Therefore, POTRA can regulate
gate dynamics, and may drive the β1-β3 switch between gate-open and gate-
closed conformations.
We are unsure why different OMPs have retained different POTRA domains. This may be
attributed to the substrate pool, which is larger for BamA with its five POTRA domains (Biochim
Biophys Acta Biomembr 2017 1859(12):2467-2482). Another possible reason could be the
exposure of bacterial insertases to harsher external environments, wherein POTRA may help
keep the BamA lumen “closed” to nonspecific entry of molecules from the external environment.
The role of POTRA domain in both bacteria and mitochondria is contrasting. In bacteria, it
assists in precursor binding, whereas it helps precursor release in mitochondria (Mol Biol Cell
2011 22(16):2823-33). We have briefly mentioned this on page 3, lines 9-11:
Sam50, the core SAM component, is a 16-stranded mOMP insertase, with one N-
terminal POlypeptide TRansport Associated (POTRA) domain located in the IMS
that facilitates precursor release (Figure 1a).
Minor:
1. Page 4, lines 15, 31, 32, and 36, It is not clear about the difference between the “path-
independent assembly” and the “path-dependent assembly”. The authors should add some
definitions of the two types of assembly.
Response page 5
Author response: We apologize for not defining the terminologies. By path-independent
folding, we refer to reversible systems that display no hysteresis. Here, the folding and unfolding
equilibria overlay, and allow for accurate measurements of thermodynamic parameters.
